In this article, some of the main points of this debate will be highlighted. The ﬁrst epidemiological studies suggesting health
implications of weight cycling were reviewed by Lissner and Brownell, when the majority of available observational evidence indi-
cated adverse consequences. Subsequently, this topic became a source of considerable controversy, and a number of investigators
continued to examine this issue, focusing on possible effects of weight cycling on metabolism, chronic disease, and mental health.
This article will offer an overview of knowledge in this area, together with some methodological controversies surrounding existing
research on weight cycling.
The Metabolic Hypothesis
Given the fact that most people who lose weight are unable to sustain their losses, a ‘metabolic’ hypothesis was formulated. It was
proposed that if weight loss dieting caused permanent decreases in metabolic rate, the weight would be easily regained and every
subsequent weight loss attempt would be more difﬁcult. In 1994, the National Task Force on the Prevention and Treatment of
Obesity in the US reviewed the evidence and reported an overall lack of support for the hypothesis that weight cycling promoted
obesity, increased body fat, or had permanent effects on metabolism. This report also concluded that the majority of available data
in animals did not independently link weight cycling to any parameter of energy balance (food intake, body composition, or energy
